title: Corporate AI
blurb: Bringing AI into a company: use cases, architecture, governance and value.

lessons.title: Why companies adopt AI
lessons.summary: The value levers behind the hype.

cards.title: Four value levers
cards.text: AI creates business value in four main ways: doing work faster and cheaper, making better decisions, improving customer experience, and enabling new products or revenue.

cards.title: Productivity
cards.text: Automating or accelerating routine knowledge work, such as reading documents, drafting, reconciling, answering standard questions, frees people for higher-value work.

cards.title: Better decisions
cards.text: Forecasting demand, prices, risk or maintenance needs more accurately reduces waste and improves margins. In trading, small forecast improvements can be worth a lot.

cards.title: Customer experience
cards.text: Faster, 24/7 answers, personalised recommendations and quicker processing of orders and claims improve satisfaction and loyalty.

cards.title: Risk and compliance
cards.text: AI can screen transactions for fraud, check contracts against policies, monitor sanctions lists and flag anomalies far faster than manual review.

cards.title: Not just cost cutting
cards.text: The strongest AI programmes treat AI as a capability for growth and better work, not just headcount reduction. Framing affects adoption: people embrace tools that help them.

cards.title: Where value concentrates
cards.text: Value tends to concentrate in core processes with high volume, repetitive judgement and lots of documents or data: finance operations, customer service, supply chain, sales and software development.

cards.title: Hype vs reality
cards.text: Many pilots never reach production. The gap is usually not the model but data, integration, process change and trust. Plan for those from day one.

cards.title: Competitive pressure
cards.text: As competitors adopt AI, the baseline for speed and cost shifts. Waiting can mean falling behind; rushing without foundations can waste money. A steady, prioritised approach wins.

cards.title: Start with the problem

items.r: "we need to cut invoice processing time by half"

cards.text: The best AI projects start from a business problem with an owner and a measurable outcome, not from a technology looking for a use.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four main AI value levers?
quiz.explain: The levers are productivity, decisions, customer experience, new revenue.

quiz.q: Why do many AI pilots fail to reach production?
options: Data, integration, process change and trust aren't addressed
quiz.explain: The model is rarely the main blocker.

quiz.q: A good AI project starts from…
options: A business problem with an owner and measurable outcome

lessons.title: Finding use cases
lessons.summary: Spotting and prioritising where AI helps.

cards.title: Look for patterns
cards.text: Good candidates involve repetitive tasks, lots of text or documents, clear rules with many exceptions, or decisions based on historical data.

cards.title: Ask the people who do the work
cards.text: The best ideas come from front-line staff who know where time is wasted. Workshops and process walkthroughs surface them quickly.

cards.title: Value vs feasibility
cards.text: Score each idea on business value and feasibility (data available, technical difficulty, risk). Start with high-value, high-feasibility ideas: quick wins.

cards.title: The feasibility checklist
cards.text: Is the data available and good enough? Can the output be checked? Is the process owner committed? Are there legal or regulatory constraints? Can it integrate with existing systems?

cards.title: Risk tier
cards.text: Classify each use case by risk: internal drafting is low risk; decisions about people (hiring, credit) or safety are high risk and need stricter controls.

cards.title: Generative vs predictive
cards.text: Choose the right tool: generative AI for language and documents; predictive ML for numbers and forecasts; rules for simple deterministic logic. Many solutions combine them.

cards.title: Copilots vs automation
cards.text: Copilots assist a person (drafting, suggesting), keeping humans in control. Automation completes tasks end-to-end. Copilots are easier to adopt first; automation delivers bigger savings once trusted.

cards.title: Use-case portfolio
cards.text: Balance a portfolio: a few quick wins to build momentum, some larger transformational bets, and enabling foundations (data, platform, skills).

cards.title: Write a one-page brief
cards.text: For each use case: problem, users, expected value, data needed, success metric, risks, owner. A one-pager forces clarity before spending money.

cards.title: Kill fast
cards.text: Not every idea works. Set a short timebox and clear success criteria for experiments, and stop those that don't meet them. Learning quickly is the goal.

quiz.q: Which ideas should usually go first?
AI deciding on job applicants is which risk tier?
quiz.explain: Decisions about people are high risk.

quiz.q: Forecasting demand is best suited to…
quiz.explain: Numbers and history suit predictive models.

lessons.title: Build, buy or partner
lessons.summary: Choosing how to get AI capabilities.

cards.title: Three options
cards.text: Buy: use AI features in software you already have or SaaS tools. Build: develop your own solutions on models and platforms. Partner: work with a specialist or integrator.

cards.title: When to buy
cards.text: Buy for common needs where you don't differentiate: email drafting, meeting notes, generic chat, standard HR or CRM features. Faster and cheaper to start.

cards.title: When to build
cards.text: Build where AI touches your competitive advantage or proprietary data, where integration with core systems is deep, or where off-the-shelf tools don't fit your process.

cards.title: Embedded AI in core systems
cards.text: ERP, CRM and productivity suites increasingly include AI (Microsoft Copilot, SAP Joule, Salesforce Einstein). Check what you already license before building.

cards.title: Platforms, not one-offs
cards.text: Building each use case from scratch is slow. A shared AI platform (model access, RAG, guardrails, monitoring) lets teams build many solutions faster and consistently.

cards.title: Vendor lock-in
cards.text: Relying on one model or vendor can be risky as the market moves fast. Abstraction layers, open standards and portable data reduce lock-in.

cards.title: Evaluating vendors
cards.text: Ask for evidence on your data: accuracy, security certifications, data handling terms, integration options, pricing at scale and roadmap.

cards.title: Total cost
cards.text: Count more than licences: integration, data preparation, change management, monitoring, support and model usage costs over several years.

cards.title: Partners
cards.text: System integrators and specialist firms bring experience and capacity. Keep core knowledge in-house so you aren't dependent on them for every change.

cards.title: Revisit regularly
cards.text: What you build today may become a commodity product next year. Review build/buy decisions as the market matures.

quiz.q: When does building usually make sense?
options: For core, differentiating processes with proprietary data

quiz.q: What reduces vendor lock-in?
options: Abstraction layers, open standards and owning your data

quiz.q: Before building a new AI tool you should check…
options: What AI features your existing software already offers
quiz.explain: Embedded AI may already cover it.

cards.title: Start from a baseline
cards.text: Measure the current process first: time per task, volume, error rate, cost, cycle time. Without a baseline you can't prove improvement.

cards.title: Time savings value

viz.f: value = volume × time saved × hourly cost × adoption

cards.text: A simple estimate: volume × time saved per item × cost per hour × adoption rate. Be conservative.

cards.title: Beyond time savings
cards.text: Include quality improvements (fewer errors), faster cycle times (cash collected sooner), risk reduction and better decisions. These are often worth more than hours saved.

cards.title: Full costs
cards.text: Include build costs, licences or model usage, integration, data preparation, change management, training and running costs for several years.

cards.title: ROI and payback
cards.text: ROI compares net gain with cost; payback is how long until cumulative value covers investment.

cards.title: Adoption drives value
cards.text: A tool nobody uses delivers nothing. Model value with realistic adoption curves, rising over months, not 100% from day one.

cards.title: Freed time must be used
cards.text: Saved hours only become value if they're redeployed: more volume handled, better service, new work, or reduced overtime and outsourcing.

cards.title: Ranges, not points
cards.text: AI outcomes are uncertain. Present low, expected and high scenarios, and the assumptions behind each.

cards.title: Measure after launch
cards.text: Track the same metrics as the baseline after launch and compare. Report real results, including what didn't work.

cards.title: Strategic value
cards.text: Some investments, such as data platforms or AI skills, don't pay back on one use case but enable many. Fund them as foundations, with a portfolio view.

quiz.q: 10,000 items, 0.2 h saved each, €50/h, 50% adoption gives about…
Why measure a baseline first?
quiz.explain: Without it, gains can't be shown.

quiz.q: Saved time becomes real value when…
options: It's redeployed to valuable work or reduces costs

cards.title: Data is the bottleneck
cards.text: For most companies, the hardest part of AI is not the model but finding, accessing, cleaning and connecting the right data.

cards.title: Know your data
cards.text: A data catalogue lists what data exists, where it lives, who owns it, what it means and how sensitive it is. Without one, teams waste weeks searching.

cards.title: Data quality dimensions
cards.text: Quality means accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness and uniqueness. A dashboard of quality scores per key dataset makes problems visible.

cards.title: Master data
cards.text: Customers, suppliers, products and materials should have one trusted version across systems. Messy master data breaks analytics and AI alike.

cards.title: Unstructured data
cards.text: Contracts, emails, PDFs and manuals hold huge value for generative AI but are often scattered across drives and mailboxes, with duplicates and outdated versions.

cards.title: Data platforms
cards.text: Modern platforms (data lakehouses such as Databricks, Microsoft Fabric or Snowflake) bring data from many systems into one governed place for analytics and AI.

cards.title: Data ownership
cards.text: Each important dataset needs a business owner accountable for its quality and access rules, supported by data stewards.

cards.title: Data products
cards.text: Treat key datasets as products: documented, quality-checked, with clear owners and service levels, so many teams can reuse them reliably.

cards.title: Lineage
cards.text: Lineage shows where data came from and how it was transformed. It's essential for trusting AI outputs and for audits.

cards.title: Classification and access
cards.text: Classify data (public, internal, confidential, restricted) and enforce access rules, so AI tools only see what each user is allowed to see.

quiz.q: What is often the hardest part of corporate AI?
options: Finding, accessing and cleaning the right data

quiz.q: What is master data?
options: The single trusted version of core entities like customers and products

quiz.q: Why classify data sensitivity?
options: So access rules can be enforced, including for AI tools
quiz.explain: Users and AI should see only what's allowed.

lessons.title: Enterprise AI architecture
lessons.summary: The building blocks of an AI platform.

cards.title: Layers of an AI platform
cards.text: A typical enterprise AI platform has: data sources, a data layer, model access, an orchestration layer (RAG, agents), guardrails, and applications, with security and monitoring across all.

cards.title: The AI gateway

steps: AI gateway: auth, routing, logging, quotas

cards.text: A central gateway sits between applications and models. It handles authentication, routing, quotas, logging, cost tracking and content filters, and lets you swap models centrally.

cards.title: Model catalogue
cards.text: Offer approved models through the gateway: a few general models of different sizes, embedding models, and specialised ones. Document which to use for what.

cards.title: Knowledge layer
cards.text: Shared RAG services index approved document collections with permissions, so every team doesn't rebuild search and chunking from scratch.

cards.title: Tools and integration
cards.text: Agents and copilots need safe access to systems: ERP, CRM, ticketing. Expose well-defined APIs or MCP servers rather than broad database access.

cards.title: Guardrails
cards.text: Input and output filters check for prompt injection, sensitive data, toxic content and policy violations. Business rules validate outputs before they reach customers or systems.

cards.title: Observability
cards.text: Log prompts, responses, tool calls, latency, costs and user feedback (with privacy controls). Traces help debug failures; dashboards show usage and spend.

cards.title: Environments
cards.text: Separate development, test and production, with evaluation gates before promotion, just like other software.

cards.title: Cloud and region

items: Encryption at rest and in transit

cards.text: Choose model hosting regions that satisfy data residency rules (for example EU data in EU regions) and contract terms that prohibit training on your data.

cards.title: Reference architecture
cards.text: Document a reference architecture and reusable templates so teams can launch new AI applications quickly within guardrails.

quiz.q: What does an AI gateway provide?
options: Central routing, auth, logging, quotas and cost tracking
quiz.explain: A control point between apps and models.

quiz.q: How should agents access ERP or CRM?
options: Through well-defined, least-privilege APIs or MCP servers

quiz.q: What do guardrails check?
options: Inputs and outputs for injection, sensitive data and policy violations
quiz.explain: They filter before and after the model.

lessons.title: AI security and privacy
lessons.summary: New risks and how to manage them.

cards.title: New attack surface
cards.text: AI systems add new risks: prompt injection, data leakage through prompts or outputs, poisoned training or retrieval data, model abuse and insecure tool access.

cards.title: Prompt injection

steps: Attacker hides instructions in a document
Guardrails and limited permissions stop harm

cards.text: Malicious instructions hidden in emails, web pages or documents can make an AI assistant reveal data or take actions. It's considered a top risk for LLM applications (OWASP).

cards.title: Data leakage
cards.text: Sensitive data can leak if users paste it into unapproved tools, if RAG ignores permissions, or if outputs include confidential details. Controls: approved tools, permission-aware retrieval and output filters.

cards.title: Shadow AI
cards.text: Employees using unapproved AI tools ("shadow AI") is common when approved options are lacking. The best defence is providing good approved tools plus clear guidance.

cards.title: Least privilege for agents
cards.text: Give AI agents the minimum access needed, scoped tokens, rate limits and approval steps for sensitive actions. Treat them like a new employee with very limited rights.

cards.title: Supply chain
cards.text: Models, libraries and plugins come from third parties. Vet sources, scan dependencies and pin versions, like any other software supply chain.

cards.title: Personal data and GDPR
cards.text: Using personal data in AI requires a lawful basis, purpose limitation, minimisation and often a data protection impact assessment (DPIA). Involve the DPO early.

cards.title: Red teaming
cards.text: Before launch, test AI apps adversarially: try injections, jailbreaks, data extraction and misuse. Fix issues and retest.

cards.title: Incident response
cards.text: Have a plan for AI incidents: harmful outputs, data exposure, agent mistakes. Be able to disable features quickly, investigate logs and notify as required.

cards.title: Security frameworks
cards.text: Use established guidance: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001 for AI management systems, plus your existing ISO 27001 controls.

quiz.q: What is shadow AI?
quiz.explain: Best countered with good approved tools.

quiz.q: Which principle limits damage from a hijacked agent?
options: Least privilege with approvals for sensitive actions

quiz.q: Which standard defines an AI management system?

lessons.title: AI governance and risk
lessons.summary: Policies, roles and the EU AI Act in practice.

cards.title: Why governance

items: incidents, or slow approvals and shadow AI

cards.text: Governance makes sure AI is used safely, legally and in line with company values, without slowing everything down. Good governance enables faster adoption by clarifying the rules.

cards.title: AI policy

items: How to propose new use cases

cards.text: A short policy covers approved tools, permitted data, human oversight, transparency, prohibited uses and how to request new use cases.

cards.title: Inventory of AI systems
cards.text: Keep a register of AI systems and use cases: purpose, owner, data used, model, risk level and controls. The EU AI Act effectively requires knowing what you deploy.

cards.title: Risk-based review
cards.text: Low-risk uses get a light self-assessment; high-risk ones go through a full review with legal, security, privacy and business experts.

cards.title: The EU AI Act for companies
cards.text: Companies are usually "deployers" of AI. For high-risk systems they must use them as instructed, ensure human oversight, monitor operation, keep logs and inform affected people. Banned practices must be avoided entirely.

cards.title: AI literacy duty
cards.text: Since February 2025, the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures to ensure sufficient AI literacy among staff who operate or use AI systems.

cards.title: Roles and responsibilities
cards.text: Typical roles: an executive sponsor, an AI governance board, use-case owners, a central AI team, plus legal, privacy, security and risk functions.

cards.title: Model risk management
cards.text: Banks and other regulated firms already manage model risk: validation, documentation, performance monitoring. Extend these practices to AI and LLMs.

cards.title: Third-party AI
cards.text: Many AI risks come through vendors. Contracts should cover data use, security, transparency, incident notification and compliance with laws like the AI Act.

cards.title: Balance speed and control
cards.text: Pre-approved patterns (approved tools, templates, low-risk categories) let most teams move fast, while scrutiny focuses on high-risk cases.

quiz.q: What should an AI inventory record?
options: Use case, owner, data, model, risk level and controls

quiz.q: Since February 2025, the EU AI Act requires deployers to ensure…
options: Sufficient AI literacy among staff using AI

quiz.q: How should governance treat low-risk use cases?
options: Give them a fast lane with light checks

cards.title: Common principles
cards.text: Most responsible AI frameworks share principles: fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety and reliability, and human oversight.

cards.title: Fairness
cards.text: Check that AI doesn't treat people unfairly based on protected characteristics or proxies. Test outcomes across groups for any use affecting people.

cards.title: Transparency
cards.text: People should know when AI is involved and, for important decisions, understand the main reasons. Internally, document how systems work and their limits.

cards.title: Accountability

items.r: "the credit team decided, using an AI recommendation"

cards.text: A named person or team is accountable for each AI system's outcomes. "The algorithm decided" is never an acceptable answer.

cards.title: Human oversight
cards.text: Decide where humans must review: before action (human-in-the-loop), monitoring with the ability to intervene (human-on-the-loop), or periodic audits.

cards.title: Reliability
cards.text: AI systems should perform consistently within their intended scope, with tested limits and graceful handling when uncertain: escalate rather than guess.

cards.title: Workforce impact
cards.text: Responsible adoption considers people: communicate openly, involve employees, invest in reskilling, and redesign roles thoughtfully.

cards.title: Environmental impact
cards.text: AI uses energy and water. Choose efficient models, avoid unnecessary use of the largest models and prefer cloud regions powered by clean energy.

cards.title: Model and system cards
cards.text: Short documents describing a system's purpose, data, performance, limitations and intended use help users and reviewers understand it.

cards.title: Trust is the goal
cards.text: Responsible AI isn't a brake; it builds the trust that lets customers, regulators and employees accept AI at scale.

quiz.q: Which is an acceptable explanation for an AI-assisted decision?
options: "The team decided using an AI recommendation"
quiz.explain: A human or team stays accountable.

quiz.q: Human-on-the-loop means…
What should an AI system do when uncertain?

cards.title: Models are living systems
cards.text: Unlike traditional software, AI behaviour depends on data and models that change. Production AI needs continuous monitoring, retraining and evaluation.

cards.title: MLOps
cards.text: MLOps applies DevOps practices to machine learning: version data and models, automate training pipelines, test before deployment and monitor in production.

cards.title: LLMOps
cards.text: For generative AI, the moving parts are prompts, retrieval indexes, tools, guardrails and model versions. All should be versioned, tested and monitored.

cards.title: Evaluation gates

steps: Ship only if equal or better

cards.text: Every change (new prompt, new model, new data) runs through automated evals before release. If quality drops, the change doesn't ship.

cards.title: Monitoring quality
cards.text: Track accuracy proxies (user feedback, correction rates, escalation rates), drift in inputs, latency, errors and cost. Sample outputs for human review.

cards.title: Data drift
cards.text: When incoming data changes (new products, new document formats, new markets), model performance can degrade silently. Drift detection alerts the team.

cards.title: Rollbacks

steps: Feature flag off or roll back

cards.text: Keep the previous version ready. If a release causes problems, roll back quickly. Feature flags let you switch AI features off without redeploying.

cards.title: Cost monitoring
cards.text: Generative AI costs scale with usage. Track spend per application and team, set budgets and alerts, and optimise prompts and model choice.

cards.title: Human feedback loops
cards.text: Corrections made by users are valuable training and evaluation data. Capture them systematically to improve prompts, retrieval and models.

cards.title: Platform teams
cards.text: A central platform team usually provides the tooling (pipelines, gateway, monitoring, eval frameworks) so product teams can focus on use cases.

quiz.q: What should happen before a new prompt version is released?
What is data drift?
options: Incoming data changing so model performance degrades

quiz.q: What lets you switch an AI feature off without redeploying?

cards.title: Pilot purgatory
cards.text: Many organisations run dozens of AI pilots that impress in demos but never scale. Common causes: no clear owner, no integration plan, unproven value and unresolved risk questions.

cards.title: Design for production from day one
cards.text: Even in a pilot, use real data, real users, the target architecture and security controls. A demo on clean sample data proves little.

cards.title: Define success upfront
cards.text: Agree measurable success criteria before starting: accuracy threshold, time saved, user satisfaction, cost per transaction.

cards.title: Integration is the work
cards.text: Value appears when AI is inside the workflow: in the ERP screen, the email client, the ticketing tool, not in a separate chat window people forget to use.

cards.title: Handle exceptions
cards.text: Design for the cases the AI can't handle: low confidence routes to humans, with an easy way to correct and learn.

cards.title: Scale step by step
cards.text: Expand gradually: one team, one region, one document type, then more. Each step reveals new edge cases and builds confidence.

cards.title: Operating ownership
cards.text: After launch someone must own it: monitoring, support, improvements and costs. Without an owner, solutions decay.

cards.title: Industrialise the pattern
cards.text: Once one use case works, turn it into a reusable pattern (document extraction, knowledge assistant, triage) and apply it across similar processes.

cards.title: Communicate wins
cards.text: Share measured results internally: hours saved, errors avoided, user stories. Visible wins build momentum and funding for the next wave.

cards.title: Stop what doesn't work
cards.text: Not every pilot should scale. A disciplined stop decision frees resources and is a sign of a healthy portfolio.

quiz.q: What is "pilot purgatory"?
options: Many pilots that never reach production
quiz.explain: Pilots stall without owners, integration and proof of value.

quiz.q: Where should an AI tool live for high adoption?
options: Inside the workflow tools people already use

quiz.q: What should happen to low-confidence AI results?

cards.title: Technology is the easy part
cards.text: AI projects fail more often because people don't adopt them than because the technology fails. Change management deserves real budget and attention.

cards.title: Address fears openly
cards.text: People worry about job security, being monitored and looking incompetent. Leaders should explain the purpose honestly and how roles will evolve.

cards.title: Champions network
cards.text: Enthusiastic early users in each team help colleagues, share tips and give feedback. Peer learning spreads faster than central training.

cards.title: Hands-on training
cards.text: Short, practical sessions with real tasks from people's own work beat generic presentations. Show before-and-after examples.

cards.title: Redesign the process
cards.text: Dropping AI into an unchanged process gives small gains. Rethinking steps, roles and approvals around AI unlocks bigger ones.

cards.title: Leaders go first
cards.text: When leaders visibly use AI tools themselves and talk about it, adoption rises. If they don't, teams conclude it isn't important.

cards.title: Measure adoption
cards.text: Track active users, frequency, use cases, satisfaction and impact. Low adoption in a team is a signal to investigate, not just push harder.

cards.title: Make it easy
cards.text: Single sign-on, integration in existing tools, prompt libraries and templates remove friction. Every extra click costs adoption.

cards.title: Celebrate and share
cards.text: Share success stories, run internal showcases or hackathons, and recognise people who find valuable new uses.

cards.title: ADKAR in brief
cards.text: A common change model: Awareness of why, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how, Ability to do it, Reinforcement to make it stick.

quiz.q: Why do many AI tools see low usage?
options: People aren't supported to change how they work

quiz.q: What is an AI champions network?
options: Early adopters who help and train colleagues

quiz.q: What does the "A" at the start of ADKAR stand for?
quiz.explain: Awareness of why change is needed.

lessons.title: Skills and operating model
lessons.summary: Who does what in an AI-enabled company.

cards.title: AI literacy for all

items: What AI can and can't do

cards.text: Everyone using AI needs basic literacy: what it can and can't do, how to prompt, how to check outputs and what data rules apply. The EU AI Act now requires it.

cards.title: Key roles
cards.text: Building AI needs a mix: product owners, data engineers, ML/AI engineers, software engineers, designers, and domain experts, plus governance roles.

cards.title: Centre of Excellence
cards.text: A central AI CoE sets standards, builds the platform, shares best practice and helps teams. It avoids duplication and inconsistent controls.

cards.title: Hub and spoke
cards.text: A common model: a central hub (platform, governance, expertise) plus spokes embedded in business units who know local processes and drive use cases.

cards.title: Global teams
cards.text: Large companies often combine global platform teams with regional delivery hubs, balancing standards with local needs and time zones.

cards.title: Upskilling engineers
cards.text: Existing developers can learn AI engineering quickly: APIs, RAG, evaluation, prompt design. Upskilling plus a few specialists often beats hiring only new experts.

cards.title: Domain experts are essential
cards.text: Accountants, traders, lawyers and engineers define what "good" looks like, label examples and validate outputs. Without them, AI solutions miss the point.

cards.title: New roles
cards.text: New roles are emerging: AI product manager, AI engineer, evaluation specialist, AI governance lead, and agent operations.

cards.title: Career paths
cards.text: As routine tasks shrink, roles shift toward judgement, exception handling, relationships and supervising AI. Clear career paths reduce anxiety and keep talent.

cards.title: Continuous learning
cards.text: AI changes fast. Build learning into the job: communities of practice, internal demos, learning budgets and time to experiment.

quiz.q: What does an AI Centre of Excellence do?
options: Sets standards, builds shared platforms and supports teams

quiz.q: In a hub-and-spoke model, spokes are…
options: AI teams embedded in business units

quiz.q: Why are domain experts essential to AI projects?
options: They define what good looks like and validate outputs

lessons.title: AI in finance and back office

cards.title: Invoice processing
cards.text: AI extracts supplier, dates, amounts, VAT and line items from invoices in any layout, matches them to purchase orders and goods receipts, and flags mismatches.

cards.title: Three-way match
cards.text: Classic accounts payable check: invoice, purchase order and goods receipt must agree on quantities and prices. AI speeds matching and explains mismatches.

cards.title: Reconciliations
cards.text: Matching bank statements, intercompany balances and ledgers is repetitive. ML can match transactions with fuzzy references and learn from past manual matches.

cards.title: Financial close
cards.text: AI can draft variance explanations, check journal entries for anomalies and summarise close status, shortening month-end.

cards.title: Cash forecasting
cards.text: ML models forecast customer payments and supplier outflows from history, improving cash and working-capital planning.

cards.title: Fraud and anomalies
cards.text: Detect duplicate invoices, unusual payments, changed bank details and suspicious vendors before money leaves.

cards.title: Expense audits
cards.text: AI reads receipts, checks them against policy and flags exceptions, so auditors review the risky few instead of sampling randomly.

cards.title: Controls and auditability
cards.text: Finance needs full traceability: every AI-proposed posting should show source documents, confidence and who approved it. Auditors must be able to follow the trail.

cards.title: ERP integration
cards.text: Value comes when AI is connected to the ERP (SAP S/4HANA, Oracle, Dynamics): reading master data, proposing postings, updating workflows.

cards.title: Measuring finance AI
cards.text: Track touchless processing rate, cycle time, error rate, cost per invoice, days to close and early-payment discounts captured.

quiz.q: What is a three-way match?
options: Matching PO, goods receipt and invoice

quiz.q: Why must finance AI keep an audit trail?
options: So auditors can trace every posting to sources and approvals

quiz.q: What does "touchless rate" measure?
options: Share of items processed without human intervention

cards.title: Demand forecasting
cards.text: ML forecasts demand using history, seasonality, prices, weather and events, improving on simple averages and helping plan production and stock.

cards.title: Supply chain visibility
cards.text: AI combines data from ERP, carriers, ports and suppliers to predict delays and suggest actions, such as rerouting or reprioritising orders.

cards.title: Logistics optimisation
cards.text: Optimisation and ML plan routes, vessel schedules, warehouse picking and truck loading, reducing cost and emissions.

cards.title: Predictive maintenance
cards.text: Sensors on machines (vibration, temperature, power) feed models that predict failures, so maintenance happens before breakdowns.

cards.title: Commodity price signals
cards.text: Models combine supply and demand data, weather, crop conditions, freight and macro indicators to support analysts' views. They inform, not replace, trading judgement.

cards.title: Satellite and weather data
cards.text: Satellite images and weather forecasts help estimate crop health and yields across regions like Brazil, the US Midwest and the Black Sea before official reports.

cards.title: Contract intelligence
cards.text: Generative AI extracts key terms from trade contracts (quantities, quality specs, shipment periods, Incoterms, demurrage, payment terms) and flags unusual clauses.

cards.title: Trade operations
cards.text: AI helps with documents (bills of lading, certificates, letters of credit), checking consistency across them and spotting discrepancies before they cause payment delays.

cards.title: Risk and compliance
cards.text: Sanctions screening, counterparty risk and vessel tracking benefit from AI that monitors news, ownership data and ship movements.

cards.title: Humans in the loop
cards.text: In trading and operations, AI provides signals and automation, while experienced people make the commercial and risk decisions.

quiz.q: What does predictive maintenance use?
In trade contracts, what is demurrage?
options: A charge per day when a vessel is delayed beyond agreed laytime

quiz.q: Who should make final trading decisions?

lessons.title: AI in customer service and sales

cards.title: Support copilots
cards.text: AI drafts replies for agents using knowledge bases and case history. Agents edit and send, handling more cases with consistent quality.

cards.title: Self-service assistants
cards.text: Customer-facing assistants answer common questions 24/7 and hand over to humans for complex or sensitive cases, with full context passed on.

cards.title: Ticket triage
cards.text: Classify incoming requests by topic, urgency and language, and route them to the right team automatically.

cards.title: Sentiment and quality
cards.text: AI analyses conversations for sentiment, recurring issues and compliance, giving managers insight across all interactions, not just samples.

cards.title: Sales assistants
cards.text: AI prepares account briefings, summarises meetings, drafts proposals and updates the CRM, giving salespeople more time with customers.

cards.title: Lead scoring
cards.text: ML scores leads by likelihood to buy, based on past wins, behaviour and firmographics, so sales focuses on the most promising.

cards.title: Pricing support
cards.text: Models suggest prices or discounts based on deal history, demand and competition, within guardrails set by the business.

cards.title: Personalisation
cards.text: Recommending relevant products and content increases conversion, but must respect privacy and avoid being intrusive.

cards.title: Be transparent
cards.text: Customers should know when they're talking to AI, and should always be able to reach a human. The EU AI Act requires disclosure for chatbots.

cards.title: Measure service AI
cards.text: Track resolution rate, handling time, customer satisfaction, escalation rate and accuracy of answers. Watch for customers giving up.

quiz.q: What does a support copilot do?
options: Drafts replies for agents to review and send

quiz.q: What must a customer-facing assistant offer?
options: A way to reach a human

quiz.q: What is ticket triage?

cards.title: Contract review
cards.text: AI extracts key clauses (term, renewal, liability, termination, governing law), compares them with your standard positions and highlights deviations for lawyers.

cards.title: Clause libraries and playbooks
cards.text: A legal playbook defines preferred, acceptable and unacceptable positions for each clause. AI applies it consistently across thousands of contracts.

cards.title: Legal research
cards.text: AI helps search case law and regulations, but citations must be verified: lawyers have been sanctioned for submitting AI-invented cases.

cards.title: Policy assistants
cards.text: Employees ask questions about HR policies, travel rules or IT procedures and get answers grounded in official documents, with links.

cards.title: Recruiting: be careful
cards.text: CV screening and candidate ranking are high-risk under the EU AI Act. Use AI to assist (writing job ads, scheduling, summarising), and keep humans making decisions, with bias testing.

cards.title: Onboarding
cards.text: AI assistants guide new employees through systems, policies and first tasks, answering questions any time.

cards.title: Learning and development
cards.text: AI creates learning content, quizzes and personalised paths, and acts as a tutor, like this app.

cards.title: Employee data privacy
cards.text: HR data is sensitive. Restrict access, minimise data, avoid emotion recognition at work (banned under the EU AI Act) and involve works councils where required.

cards.title: Compliance monitoring
cards.text: AI tracks regulatory changes, maps them to internal policies and flags gaps, helping compliance teams keep up.

cards.title: Lawyers stay accountable
cards.text: AI speeds legal work, but professional responsibility stays with lawyers. Use it for first drafts, review and research support, with expert sign-off.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, AI that ranks job candidates is…
What does a legal playbook define?
options: Preferred, acceptable and unacceptable clause positions

quiz.q: Which practice is banned at work under the EU AI Act?

cards.title: Coding assistants
cards.text: Tools like GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code suggest code, explain it, write tests and fix bugs, inside the developer's editor or terminal.

cards.title: Productivity gains
cards.text: Controlled studies have found developers complete some coding tasks substantially faster with AI assistants, though gains vary by task, experience and codebase.

cards.title: Coding agents
cards.text: Agents take a task (an issue or ticket), plan changes across files, run tests and open a pull request for human review.

cards.title: Code review still matters
cards.text: AI-generated code can contain bugs, security issues or licence problems. Keep code review, tests and security scanning in the pipeline.

cards.title: Legacy modernisation
cards.text: AI helps understand and document legacy code (COBOL, old ABAP), suggest migrations and generate tests, speeding up modernisation projects like S/4HANA moves.

cards.title: Documentation
cards.text: AI writes and updates documentation, API descriptions and runbooks from code and commit history, reducing a chore developers often skip.

cards.title: Testing
cards.text: AI generates unit tests, test data and edge cases, raising coverage quickly. Developers still check the tests actually test the right thing.

cards.title: Low-code and citizen developers
cards.text: AI makes it easier for non-developers to build automations and small apps, but governance is needed for security, data access and maintenance.

cards.title: Security of AI-written code
cards.text: Watch for hard-coded secrets, injection flaws, outdated libraries and hallucinated package names that attackers might register.

cards.title: Measuring engineering impact
cards.text: Track cycle time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, developer satisfaction and time spent on toil, not lines of code generated.

quiz.q: What should happen to AI-generated code before merging?
options: Human review, tests and security scanning

quiz.q: What is a "hallucinated package" risk?
options: AI suggesting a non-existent library name that attackers could register

quiz.q: Which is a good measure of AI's engineering impact?
options: Cycle time and change failure rate

cards.title: Outcome over activity
cards.text: Count outcomes (cost saved, revenue gained, errors avoided, time to serve customers), not activity (number of prompts, pilots launched, users invited).

cards.title: Three levels of metrics
cards.text: Track usage (are people using it?), performance (is it accurate and fast?) and business impact (is it creating value?).

cards.title: Productivity metrics
cards.text: Time per task, throughput per person, touchless rates, backlog size and cycle times show productivity effects.

cards.title: Quality metrics
cards.text: Error rates, rework, compliance findings and customer complaints show whether AI improves or harms quality.

cards.title: Financial metrics
cards.text: Translate gains into money: cost avoided, revenue uplift, working capital released, risk losses avoided, and compare with full costs.

cards.title: Control groups
cards.text: Where possible, compare teams or periods with and without AI. Otherwise improvements may be due to other changes.

cards.title: Dashboards
cards.text: A shared AI value dashboard shows each use case's adoption, quality and value against targets, building transparency for leadership.

cards.title: Leading indicators
cards.text: Value often lags. Early signals like adoption, satisfaction and reduced handling time predict later financial results.

cards.title: Honest reporting
cards.text: Report what didn't work, not just successes. Credibility with finance and leadership comes from realistic numbers.

cards.title: Portfolio view
cards.text: Manage AI as a portfolio: some use cases deliver big wins, many modest gains, some fail. The total portfolio return is what matters.

quiz.q: Which is an outcome metric?
Why use control groups?
options: To separate AI's effect from other changes

quiz.q: What is a leading indicator of AI value?

cards.title: Strategy starts with business goals
cards.text: An AI strategy should serve the company strategy: growth, efficiency, risk, customer experience. Each AI initiative links to a business goal.

cards.title: Ambition levels
cards.text: Companies range from experimenting, to scaling selected use cases, to transforming core processes and business models with AI.

cards.title: The roadmap
cards.text: A roadmap sequences use cases and foundations over 12–36 months, with waves: quick wins first, foundations in parallel, bigger transformations later.

cards.title: Foundations in parallel
cards.text: Data, platform, governance, security and skills must be built alongside use cases, not after. Each wave of use cases funds and uses the foundations.

cards.title: Operating model
cards.text: Decide who funds, builds, owns and governs AI: central, federated or hybrid. Hybrid hub-and-spoke is common in large global companies.

cards.title: Partnerships
cards.text: Strategic partners (cloud providers, model providers, integrators, startups) speed delivery. Keep architecture and key skills in-house.

cards.title: Funding model
cards.text: Fund foundations centrally, use cases by business units (with central co-funding to start), and review the portfolio quarterly.

cards.title: Agents and the future
cards.text: As agents mature, more end-to-end processes may be automated with human oversight. Prepare now: clean APIs, clear processes, good data and governance for autonomous actions.

cards.title: Stay adaptable
cards.text: Models, prices and regulations change quickly. Revisit the strategy at least yearly, keep architecture flexible and avoid betting everything on one vendor.

cards.title: People at the centre
cards.text: The companies that win with AI combine technology with people who know the business, trust built through responsible practices, and a culture of learning.

quiz.q: What should an AI strategy serve?
quiz.explain: AI is a means, not the end.

quiz.q: When should foundations (data, platform, governance) be built?
How often should the AI strategy be revisited?
